No Result View All Result Home News Politics Business Sport Football Health Entertainment Education Opinion Editorial Columns Others LeVogue Magazine Conferences National Economy Contact Us Hausa Edition Home News Politics Business Sport Football Health Entertainment Education Opinion Editorial Columns Others LeVogue Magazine Conferences National Economy Contact Us No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Lagos Luxury Property Market Battles Rising Service Charges, Mounting Vacancies by Sani Shehu 9 minutes ago in Business Share on WhatsApp Share on Facebook Share on X Telegram Landlords and property investors in Eko Atlantic City, Oniru and other parts of Lagos’ emerging waterfront real estate corridor are increasingly battling rising service charges and mounting vacancies, as the cost of maintaining luxury residential developments erodes rental income and makes long-term letting less attractive.
The growing disparity between rental income and property maintenance expenses is creating a difficult investment environment, particularly for owners who have invested heavily in high-end apartments but are struggling to achieve returns commensurate with their investments.
In some developments, annual service charges covering electricity, water treatment, facility management, estate security, waste disposal and maintenance of common areas have become so substantial that landlords are increasingly reconsidering conventional residential letting.
A real estate broker operating in Victoria Island, who requested anonymity, told LEADERSHIP that the financial implications of these charges were making some long-term rental arrangements unattractive.
“If service charge is N12 million to N20 million annually and achievable long-let rent is N25 million to N35 million, the landlord’s net is squeezed,” the broker said.
“Rather than discount rent and still pay service charge from his pocket, many prefer to leave the flat empty, or pivot to short-let at $400-$700 per night.”
The situation highlights a growing concern in Lagos’ luxury residential market, where the financial attractiveness of a property increasingly depends not only on its rental value but also on the recurring expenses required to keep it operational.
A Lagos service-charge analysis published by Brick & Click Realty in August 2026 provides an indication of the scale of the maintenance burden across premium residential locations.
According to the firm’s Lagos Service Charge Report, annual service charges for one- and two-bedroom apartments in serviced Oniru developments range between N1.2 million and N2.5 million, while three-bedroom apartments attract between N2 million and N4 million.
For apartments with four bedrooms and above, the estimated annual charges range between N3.5 million and N6 million.
The report puts corresponding annual charges for four-bedroom and larger apartments in serviced Banana Island developments at between N7 million and N12 million.
Electricity generation, water treatment, security, cleaning, waste management, lift maintenance, amenities and sinking funds for major repairs were identified as important components of residential service-charge budgets.
Although the figures represent indicative market estimates rather than verified invoices for individual developments, they demonstrate how the cost of maintaining premium residential facilities can constitute a substantial recurring expense for property owners and occupants.
The pressure is not peculiar to Lagos’ luxury residential market. Facility management professionals say rising costs of energy, labour, imported equipment and maintenance materials are making it increasingly difficult to sustain residential and commercial properties without reviewing service charges.
Chief Executive Officer of Solid Foundation Group, Adetoun Otepola, identified diesel as one of the biggest contributors to the rising cost of maintaining properties, explaining that it powers several essential services within residential and commercial developments.
Speaking on the pressure of rising operating expenses on facility management, she said diesel was required to power common areas, water treatment plants, security systems and other essential facilities.
“The price of diesel has gone up. Diesel comes first in the maintenance costs that you have. We use it to power common areas for electricity, water treatment plants, security systems and other essential services. So, maintenance costs are on the rise,” Otepola said.
She added that rising prices of lubricants, spare parts and logistics, alongside increasing wage demands, were further compounding the financial burden on facility managers.
Her assessment explains why maintaining luxury residential developments has become increasingly expensive, particularly where residents expect uninterrupted power supply, treated water, functioning elevators and round-the-clock security.
The affected properties are concentrated along the stretch linking Ahmadu Bello Way, Oniru, Eko Atlantic City and Bluewater Okunde, an emerging luxury real estate corridor described by Palton Morgan Holdings in its September 2026 Editorial Guide as the New Victoria Island.
The corridor has attracted considerable investor attention in recent years, supported by infrastructure developments, luxury residential projects and expectations surrounding the 47.47-kilometre Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway.
Land values in the area have also recorded substantial appreciation. A parcel of approximately 2,400 square metres in Bluewater Okunde, which reportedly traded for about N800 million, is now valued at more than N5 billion.
However, the appreciation in property values has not necessarily translated into corresponding improvements in rental yields, exposing a growing disconnect between the capital value of waterfront properties and their ability to generate regular rental income.
Market data suggest that some of Lagos’ most expensive residential locations do not necessarily offer the strongest rental returns.
Rental-yield data compiled by Stears showed that Oniru recorded a rental yield of 4.88 per cent, compared with 4.59 per cent in Victoria Island and 3.09 per cent in Ikoyi. Chevron recorded the highest yield among the locations examined, at 5.85 per cent.
Speaking in a media chat, Principal Partner of Ubosi Eleh & Company, an estate surveying and valuation firm, Mr. Chudi Ubosi, explained that residential rents had increased by between 50 and 200 per cent over the preceding 24 months, attributing the increases largely to inflation and the rising cost of building materials, which had pushed up construction expenses.
His assessment provides context for the difficulties confronting landlords, as the cost of developing, operating and maintaining residential properties continues to influence the financial calculations of investors.
More specifically, Co-founder and Chief Operating Officer of Brick & Click Realty, Oluwaseyi Adaralegbe, highlighted the relatively low rental-yield characteristics of Lagos’ ultra-prime residential market in the firm’s Q3 2026 Lagos Property Market Outlook.
The report estimated gross rental yields in the ultra-prime island segment, comprising Banana Island, Eko Atlantic and Old Ikoyi, at between 3.0 and 4.8 per cent, compared with 3.8 to 6.0 per cent for the prime island and waterfront segment, which includes Victoria Island, Parkview and Lekki Phase 1.
It explained that ultra-prime locations generally command higher property values but offer relatively lower rental yields, while some outer residential corridors provide stronger income returns.
Importantly, these are gross yields calculated before management expenses and applicable taxes, meaning the actual returns available to landlords could be considerably lower after service charges and other operating costs are deducted.
Adaralegbe advised owners of ultra-prime properties to prioritise tenant retention rather than maximise rental rates, explaining that the tenant pool in the segment was relatively thin and that the cost of leaving an apartment vacant could outweigh the additional income expected from a rent increase.
His position presents a different investment calculation for landlords who would rather keep their properties unoccupied than accept lower rental offers.
In a market where the number of prospective tenants capable of paying premium rents is limited, prolonged vacancies could ultimately undermine the returns owners are seeking to protect.
The financial challenge is particularly relevant to developments such as Azuri Towers, Eko Pearl Towers and Pan Atlantic Towers, alongside newer projects including Paramount Twin Towers in the Oniru Waterfront and Nautica Rise in Oniru.
These developments operate within a high-end property segment where residents expect uninterrupted electricity, treated water, sophisticated security systems and professionally managed facilities.
For properties situated on reclaimed waterfront land, maintenance requirements may also extend to specialised infrastructure associated with coastal protection and the management of the surrounding environment, depending on the applicable development and estate arrangements.
These facilities come at a cost, and property owners may be required to meet their share of maintenance obligations whether or not their apartments are occupied.
In Eko Atlantic City, where luxury apartments are marketed at prices ranging from approximately $659,400 to $5 million, the financial burden of maintaining residential towers has become an important consideration for investors seeking long-term tenants.
Facility manager, Musa Ogundimu, said that for prospective tenants, the actual cost of securing accommodation in these developments went beyond the advertised rental price.
He noted that once annual service charges and other associated obligations were factored in, the overall cost of occupancy could become prohibitive, particularly for individuals and corporate tenants seeking long-term accommodation.
Ogundimu added that the situation had also raised questions about the adequacy of maintenance budgeting and the extent to which property owners and residents participated in decisions concerning service charges.
Similarly, Managing Director of West Norwood Realty, Alfred Osagie, said facility managers were finding it increasingly difficult to operate within existing maintenance budgets because of persistent increases in the cost of providing services.
According to him, maintenance costs had risen by an average of 30 per cent year-on-year over the preceding three years, making it difficult to sustain facilities where property owners expected operational expenses to remain unchanged.
Osagie also identified inadequate consideration of life-cycle maintenance costs during property development as an underlying problem, noting that some owners and developers did not fully appreciate the financial resources required to keep their facilities operational.
“Properties and estates are like humans. If somebody is sick and the person goes to the hospital, the doctor will not ask how much is in your account. The challenge is that people go into estates without understanding what it requires, and so there is always pressure to be able to work with a particular amount,” he said.
He advocated greater involvement of residents and tenants in preparing maintenance budgets, arguing that transparency would make it easier for occupants to understand the reasons behind service-charge adjustments.
“The budget must be done with the residents. They must understand why, where materials are purchased from and what we are using them for. It makes it easier to match the level of service to the quality of the asset, the maintenance demand of the asset and the financial capacity of the facility management companies,” Osagie said.
His position highlights an important dimension of the service-charge debate: increasing maintenance costs do not automatically justify every amount demanded from residents.
Facility managers also have a responsibility to demonstrate how funds are utilised and whether the services delivered correspond with the charges collected.
Former President of the International Facility Management Association (IFMA), Nigeria Chapter, Olalekan Akinwumi, similarly emphasised transparency in managing service charges, urging facility managers to provide tenants with regular maintenance reports.
He said rising maintenance costs had made budget compliance increasingly difficult, but argued that residents would be more willing to accommodate necessary adjustments when they understood how the money collected was being spent.
“The key word in budgeting is transparency. If people somehow feel that they don’t really understand what you are doing, then you are creating problems. Service charge is something that is a headache. At the same time, when you are transparent with it and you carry them along, they will understand,” Akinwumi said.
He also advocated alternative energy sources and more efficient generator management to reduce expenditure on diesel.
According to him, facilities could combine inverter and solar systems with generators to reduce the number of hours generators operate, thereby lowering energy costs without necessarily compromising essential services.
Also speaking, former President of the Association of Facilities Management Practitioners of Nigeria (AFMPN), Dr. Paul Erubami, identified energy as a major contributor to rising facility management costs.
He said energy accounted for more than 60 per cent of total facility management costs in many developments, explaining that escalating fuel prices and unreliable electricity supply were forcing operators to negotiate service-charge adjustments with residents.
“It’s a daunting challenge, and consumers are already feeling the strain. Their incomes are not increasing, while facility managers are grappling with shrinking margins. Both demand and supply sides are affected by the sudden onset of this global crisis, which has triggered rapid changes that no one was prepared for,” Erubami said.
His observation underscores the difficult position occupied by facility managers, who must maintain essential services while dealing with residents whose capacity to absorb additional charges is also constrained by economic realities.
For investors, the situation presents a growing dilemma. While cutting maintenance expenditure may reduce service charges in the short term, inadequate maintenance could compromise the quality, safety and long-term value of expensive residential assets.
The growing pressure is also encouraging some investors to reconsider their letting strategies, with short-term accommodation emerging as an alternative to conventional residential leases.
Rather than committing an apartment to an annual tenancy at a discounted rate, some landlords believe they could generate better income through short-let arrangements, particularly in locations with strong demand from corporate visitors, expatriates and tourists.
However, higher nightly rates do not automatically translate into better annual returns, as short-let operators must contend with occupancy fluctuations, cleaning, furnishing, utilities, booking commissions, maintenance and management expenses.
Nigeria Property Centre’s Q4 2026 property market report, published in October, put the median asking price for short-let accommodation in Lagos at ₦150,000 per night.
The platform also reported a gross rental yield of 7.14 per cent for four-bedroom properties in Lagos. However, such gross-yield calculations do not necessarily reflect the actual returns landlords receive after accounting for service charges, vacancies, maintenance and other operating expenses.
The trend is particularly noticeable around the Landmark Village axis, where short-let operators and property market observers, including Estate Intel, have reported growing investor interest in holding apartments for short-term accommodation, occasional personal use or as stores of value.
Diaspora investors, who constitute part of the ownership base in the emerging waterfront market, are also said to have some properties with relatively low occupancy, reflecting the tendency of certain buyers to acquire luxury apartments primarily for asset preservation and future appreciation rather than immediate rental income.
Nevertheless, the growing preference for vacant apartments or short-let arrangements raises questions about the long-term sustainability of the rental market in the corridor.
For landlords, leaving an apartment unoccupied does not necessarily eliminate their financial obligations. Depending on the applicable estate management arrangements, service charges and other maintenance costs may continue to accrue even when there is no tenant occupying the property.
This means property owners must weigh the cost of maintaining vacant apartments against the possibility of accepting lower rents to secure long-term occupants.
The situation also presents a challenge for developers and facility managers, as high service charges could influence the willingness of prospective buyers and tenants to commit to luxury residential properties, particularly when the costs are not matched by corresponding rental returns and service quality.
For investors assessing opportunities in Eko Atlantic City, Oniru and the wider New Victoria Island corridor, the emerging service-charge challenge underscores the need to look beyond property acquisition costs and projected capital appreciation.
While the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway and other infrastructure developments could strengthen the long-term investment appeal of the waterfront corridor, the ability of properties to generate sustainable rental income remains an important consideration.
Ultimately, the question confronting investors is whether the corridor’s attraction lies primarily in long-term capital appreciation or in its capacity to deliver consistent rental yields after operating expenses.
Until the relationship between service charges, rental prices and occupancy levels becomes more favourable, some luxury apartment owners may continue to regard an empty property as a more attractive option than a long-term tenancy that leaves little or no meaningful return.
